question: What is a large language model and how does it generate text?
directAnswer: A large language model (LLM) is a neural network trained on huge amounts of text to predict the next token given the tokens that came before it. It does not retrieve stored answers; instead it produces one token at a time, appends that token to the input, and repeats, which is called autoregressive generation. Each step outputs a probability distribution over the entire vocabulary, and a sampling strategy picks the next token from that distribution. Everything an agent does, from answering a question to calling a tool, ultimately rides on this next-token prediction loop.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs:
An LLM is a function that maps a sequence of tokens to a probability distribution over the next token. Conceptually generation looks like:
tokens = tokenize(prompt)
while not done:
    logits = model(tokens)         # scores for every vocab token
    probs = softmax(logits[-1])    # distribution for next position
    next = sample(probs)           # pick one token
    tokens.append(next)
The loop stops on a stop token or a length limit.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: LLMs exist because next-token prediction turns out to be a remarkably general objective: to predict text well the model must implicitly learn grammar, facts, reasoning patterns, and formats. Training one big model on broad data and then prompting it is far cheaper and more flexible than building a separate system for every task, which is why a single model can chat, summarize, translate, and drive an agent.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The model is built from transformer layers using self-attention, which lets every token attend to the others so context is taken into account. During training it adjusts billions of parameters to minimize the error of its next-token predictions across the corpus. At inference the parameters are frozen and only the forward pass runs: it computes logits, converts them to probabilities, samples a token, and feeds the extended sequence back in until a stopping condition is met.

whyImportant: Understanding that an LLM is fundamentally a next-token predictor is the foundation of everything in agent engineering, because it explains why prompting, context, and sampling matter so much. It clarifies why the model can hallucinate, why it has no memory between calls, and why output is probabilistic. Interviewers ask this to confirm you reason about the model mechanistically rather than treating it as a magic oracle.
realWorldExample: When you ask an assistant to write a function, it does not look up the function in a database. It generates it token by token, choosing each next token based on your prompt and everything it has produced so far. This is why the same prompt can yield slightly different code on different runs and why a well-structured prompt so strongly steers the result.

nestedTopics.title: Autoregressive generation
nestedTopics.explanation: The model generates left to right, one token at a time, feeding each new token back into the input for the next step. This sequential dependence is why longer outputs cost proportionally more compute and why the model cannot revise earlier tokens once they are emitted.

nestedTopics.title: The transformer and attention
nestedTopics.explanation: LLMs use transformer layers whose self-attention mechanism lets each position weigh the relevance of every other position in the context. Attention is what allows the model to connect a pronoun to its referent or a question to relevant earlier details, giving it context-aware behavior.

nestedTopics.title: Logits and the softmax
nestedTopics.explanation: At each step the model outputs a raw score, or logit, for every token in its vocabulary, and a softmax converts those scores into a probability distribution that sums to one. The sampling strategy then selects a token from this distribution, which is where temperature and top-p come into play.

followUps.question: Does the model remember previous conversations between separate API calls?
followUps.answer: No. An LLM is stateless across calls; it has no built-in memory of past requests. Anything it appears to remember within a conversation is because the entire prior conversation is resent as part of the prompt on each new call. If you start a fresh call without including earlier messages, the model knows nothing about them. This is why agent frameworks explicitly manage conversation history and why context windows and token budgets matter so much: memory is something you construct by including the right text in the prompt, not something the model retains on its own.

followUps.question: Why can an LLM produce different answers to the same prompt?
followUps.answer: Because generation is probabilistic. At each step the model outputs a probability distribution over possible next tokens, and unless you force deterministic decoding, the sampling step randomly selects among the likely candidates. With a non-zero temperature or top-p sampling, different runs can pick different tokens early on, and because each token conditions the next, small early differences can compound into noticeably different outputs. Setting temperature to zero (greedy decoding) makes it far more deterministic, though exact reproducibility can still be affected by hardware and batching details.

question: What is a token and why do tokens matter for cost and context?
directAnswer: A token is the unit of text an LLM actually processes: not a character and not always a whole word, but a chunk produced by the model's tokenizer, often a common word or a word fragment. Models read and write in tokens, and both pricing and the context window are measured in tokens rather than words or characters. A rough rule of thumb for English is that one token is about four characters, or roughly three quarters of a word. Because every input and output token is counted, understanding tokens is essential for controlling cost and staying within limits.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs:
A tokenizer splits text into tokens and maps each to an integer id. For example the word 'tokenization' might split into 'token' and 'ization', while a common word like 'the' is a single token. Conceptually:
text -> tokenizer -> [1123, 2340, 98] -> model
The model only ever sees these integer ids, never raw characters directly.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Tokenization exists as a compromise between character-level and word-level processing. Characters make sequences too long and slow; whole words make the vocabulary enormous and can't handle unseen words. Subword tokenization, such as byte-pair encoding, gives a manageable fixed vocabulary that can still represent any text by combining pieces, which is efficient for both training and inference.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The tokenizer is learned from data by repeatedly merging the most frequent character pairs into subword units until it reaches a target vocabulary size. Common words become single tokens while rare words split into several. At inference the input text is tokenized into ids, the model processes them, and its output ids are detokenized back into text. Every one of those input and output tokens counts toward the context window and the bill.

whyImportant: Tokens are the currency of LLM systems, so an agent engineer must think in tokens to reason about cost, latency, and context limits. Misjudging token counts leads to truncated prompts, unexpected bills, or requests that exceed the model's window. Interviewers probe this to see whether you can budget context deliberately rather than guessing by word count.
realWorldExample: Suppose you paste a 50-page document into a prompt to summarize it. Before sending, a careful engineer estimates the token count, because that document might be 30,000 tokens, which affects both whether it fits in the context window and how much the call costs. If it is too large, you must chunk it or use retrieval instead of stuffing everything in, a decision driven entirely by token accounting.

nestedTopics.title: Subword tokenization
nestedTopics.explanation: Modern tokenizers split text into subword units so that common words are single tokens and rare or novel words are broken into smaller pieces. This keeps the vocabulary bounded while still being able to encode any string, including code, emoji, and other languages, though non-English text often uses more tokens per word.

nestedTopics.title: Tokens versus words and characters
nestedTopics.explanation: There is no fixed conversion, but a common English estimate is about four characters or three quarters of a word per token. Whitespace, punctuation, and capitalization all affect the split, and code or unusual formatting can tokenize less efficiently than plain prose.

nestedTopics.title: Why token counts drive cost
nestedTopics.explanation: APIs bill separately for input (prompt) tokens and output (completion) tokens, often at different rates. Since the model must process every input token and generate every output token, both directly consume compute, which is why the token count, not the character or word count, determines the price of a call.

followUps.question: Why do input and output tokens sometimes have different prices?
followUps.answer: Because they involve different amounts of work. Input tokens are processed in a single forward pass over the whole prompt, which can be parallelized efficiently across the sequence. Output tokens, by contrast, must be generated one at a time autoregressively, where each new token requires another pass conditioned on all previous tokens, so generation is inherently sequential and often more expensive per token. Providers reflect this asymmetry in pricing, typically charging more for output tokens. It's a practical reason to keep responses concise when you don't need long output, since output tokens frequently dominate the cost of a call.

followUps.question: How would you estimate token count before sending a request?
followUps.answer: The most accurate way is to run the exact tokenizer the model uses, since token boundaries differ between model families; many providers publish a tokenizer library or a counting endpoint for this. When you only need a rough estimate, you can approximate English text at about four characters per token or three quarters of a word per token and add a margin. For agent systems it's good practice to count tokens explicitly rather than guess, especially when assembling prompts from documents or long histories, so you can trim or chunk before you hit the context limit or overspend.

question: What is the context window and what happens when you exceed it?
directAnswer: The context window is the maximum number of tokens a model can consider at once, counting both the input prompt and the tokens it generates. It is a hard limit set by the model architecture, ranging from a few thousand tokens in older models to hundreds of thousands or more in newer ones. Everything the model can 'see', the system prompt, conversation history, tool definitions, retrieved documents, and its own output, must fit within this budget. If you exceed it, the request is rejected or the oldest content is dropped, so managing the window is a core agent engineering task.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs:
The context window is a token budget shared by input and output. Conceptually:
context_window >= tokens(system_prompt)
                 + tokens(history)
                 + tokens(tools)
                 + tokens(user_message)
                 + tokens(model_output)
If the sum would exceed the limit, something has to give.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: The window exists because the transformer's attention and memory cost grow with sequence length, historically quadratically, so there is a practical ceiling on how many tokens the model can process at once. The limit is a trade-off between capability, speed, and cost: larger windows let the model use more context but require more compute and money per call.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: When you send a request, the provider tokenizes everything and checks that the total plus the space reserved for the response fits the window. If the input alone exceeds the limit, the call errors out. If it fits but leaves little room, the model can only generate a short response before hitting the ceiling. Agent frameworks handle this by trimming or summarizing old history, using retrieval to include only relevant chunks, and reserving headroom for the output.

whyImportant: The context window is one of the tightest real constraints in agent design, dictating how much history, how many tool results, and how much retrieved data you can supply. Overrunning it causes errors or silent loss of important information, degrading the agent's behavior. Interviewers ask this to see whether you plan context as a finite resource rather than assuming unlimited memory.
realWorldExample: In a long customer-support conversation, the running dialogue plus tool outputs can grow until it approaches the model's window. A well-built agent detects this and summarizes older turns into a compact recap, keeping recent messages verbatim, so the conversation can continue without hitting the limit or losing the thread. Without such management, the agent would eventually error out or start forgetting the earliest, sometimes crucial, details.

nestedTopics.title: Shared budget for input and output
nestedTopics.explanation: The window is not just for the prompt; the tokens the model generates also count against it. This means a very large prompt can leave too little room for a full answer, so you must reserve space for the expected output when you size the input.

nestedTopics.title: Everything competes for space
nestedTopics.explanation: System instructions, conversation history, tool schemas, retrieved documents, and the current user message all draw from the same budget. As one grows, less is available for the others, which forces deliberate trade-offs about what to include on each call.

nestedTopics.title: Strategies when context is tight
nestedTopics.explanation: Common tactics include trimming the oldest turns, summarizing history into a compact form, and using retrieval to pull in only the most relevant passages instead of entire documents. Each keeps the agent within budget while preserving the information that matters most.

followUps.question: If a model has a large context window, should you always fill it?
followUps.answer: No, for several reasons. First, every token you include costs money and adds latency, so stuffing the window is wasteful if much of the content is irrelevant. Second, models can struggle to use very long contexts effectively, sometimes paying less attention to information buried in the middle, so more context does not always mean better answers. Third, a bloated prompt can dilute the important instructions and increase the chance the model gets distracted. The better approach is to include only what is relevant, often via retrieval, and keep the prompt focused, treating the large window as headroom rather than a target to fill.

followUps.question: How do agents handle conversations longer than the context window?
followUps.answer: They actively manage history rather than sending everything. Common techniques include sliding-window truncation, where only the most recent turns are kept verbatim; summarization, where older turns are compressed into a short recap that preserves key facts and decisions; and external memory, where important information is stored outside the model and retrieved on demand. Many agents combine these: keep recent messages, a running summary of older ones, and a retrieval step for relevant long-term facts. The goal is to stay within the token budget while preserving the information the agent actually needs to continue coherently.

question: What are messages and roles in a chat completion API?
directAnswer: Chat-based LLM APIs structure the prompt as a list of messages, each tagged with a role that tells the model who is speaking. The common roles are system, which sets overall behavior and instructions; user, which carries the human's input; and assistant, which holds the model's replies. Agent APIs also add tool or function roles to carry tool call requests and their results. On each call you send the full message list, and the model generates the next assistant message, so the roles give conversation structure and let the model distinguish instructions from dialogue.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs:
A request is an ordered list of role-tagged messages. For example:
[
  {"role": "system",    "content": "You are a concise assistant."},
  {"role": "user",      "content": "What is 2 + 2?"},
  {"role": "assistant", "content": "4"},
  {"role": "user",      "content": "And times 3?"}
]
The model reads all of it and produces the next assistant message.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Roles exist so the model can tell apart persistent instructions, user requests, and its own prior responses, which plain concatenated text cannot express cleanly. The system role gives a dedicated place for behavior and policy that should govern the whole conversation, while alternating user and assistant messages represent the turn-taking of a dialogue. Tool roles were added so the same structure can carry the request-and-response cycle of function calling.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The API serializes the message list into a single formatted sequence, using special tokens or a template that marks role boundaries, and feeds it to the model. The model was trained on this format, so it treats the system message as authoritative context, the user messages as things to respond to, and the assistant messages as its own voice. It then generates a new assistant message conditioned on the whole list, which you append and resend on the next turn.

whyImportant: The message and role structure is the primary interface you use to control an agent, so understanding it is fundamental. Knowing where to put durable instructions versus per-turn input, and how tool results flow back as messages, is essential to building anything beyond a single call. Interviewers ask this to confirm you understand the conversational contract the whole agent loop is built on.
realWorldExample: A coding assistant places its persona and rules in the system message, such as 'always return runnable code and explain briefly'. Each user question and each of the assistant's answers are appended in order, and when the assistant calls a tool, the tool's output comes back as a tool-role message. On the next turn the entire list is resent so the model has the full, correctly attributed conversation to reason over.

nestedTopics.title: The system role
nestedTopics.explanation: The system message sets the model's persona, constraints, and standing instructions for the whole conversation. Because it is treated as high-priority context, it is where you put behavior rules, output format requirements, and safety guidance that should persist across every turn rather than being repeated in each user message.

nestedTopics.title: User and assistant turns
nestedTopics.explanation: User messages carry human input and assistant messages carry the model's responses, alternating to form the dialogue. Including prior assistant messages is what gives the model continuity, since it is otherwise stateless; the history is the conversation as far as the model is concerned.

nestedTopics.title: Tool and function roles
nestedTopics.explanation: Agent APIs extend the roles to carry tool interactions: the assistant can emit a structured tool call, and the tool's result is fed back as a message with a tool role. This lets the model's action and the environment's response live in the same message list, driving the agent loop.

followUps.question: What is the difference between putting instructions in the system message versus the user message?
followUps.answer: The system message is designed for durable, high-priority instructions that should shape the model's behavior across the entire conversation, such as its persona, tone, output format, and safety rules. It is generally given more weight and is the right place for things that must not drift as the dialogue goes on. The user message carries the specific request for that turn, the actual task or question. Mixing standing rules into every user message is repetitive and less reliable, while omitting a system message and hoping the user text alone controls behavior tends to be weaker. As a rule, put policy and persona in the system role and the concrete ask in the user role.

followUps.question: Why must you resend the whole message history on each call?
followUps.answer: Because the model is stateless between API calls and retains no memory of prior turns on its own. The only way it knows what was said earlier is if that history is included in the request. So to continue a conversation coherently, you append each new user message and each model response to the list and send the full list every time. This is also why long conversations eventually strain the context window and require trimming or summarization: the entire remembered dialogue physically travels in each request, and it all counts against the token budget.

question: What is a prompt and what makes a prompt effective?
directAnswer: A prompt is the text input you give an LLM to steer its output, and since the model only responds to what it is given, the prompt is your main lever of control. An effective prompt is clear and specific about the task, provides the necessary context, states the desired format, and often includes examples of the expected output. Because the model predicts a continuation of your input, ambiguity or missing context leads to guesses, while precise instructions and constraints reliably shape the result. Good prompting is less about clever phrasing and more about giving the model exactly what it needs to succeed.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs:
A prompt is everything you send that the model conditions on. A weak prompt might be 'summarize this', while a strong one specifies audience, length, and format:
Summarize the text below for a busy executive.
Use at most three bullet points, each one sentence.
Text: <...>
The added structure removes guesswork.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Prompting exists because the model is a general predictor with no inherent knowledge of your specific goal. The prompt is how you convert that general capability into a task-specific behavior without retraining. Since a single model must serve countless tasks, the prompt is the flexible, per-request instruction that adapts the model to what you want right now.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The model reads the prompt as context and generates the most likely continuation given that context and its training. Clear instructions, relevant context, explicit format requirements, and examples all shift the probability distribution toward the output you want. Techniques like giving a role, breaking the task into steps, and showing input-output examples work because they make the desired continuation more probable and reduce the model's need to guess your intent.

whyImportant: Prompting is the day-to-day craft of working with LLMs, and the quality of prompts often matters more than the choice of model for a given task. An agent's reliability depends heavily on well-structured system and task prompts. Interviewers ask this to see whether you approach prompting systematically, with clear instructions and format control, rather than trial-and-error incantations.
realWorldExample: Asking a model to 'extract the total from this invoice' often yields inconsistent formats. Rewriting the prompt to 'Return only the invoice total as a JSON object like {"total": 0.00}, with no other text' makes the output predictable and parseable. That single change, adding a precise format instruction and an example, is the difference between an output you can plug into code and one you have to clean up by hand.

nestedTopics.title: Clarity and specificity
nestedTopics.explanation: The most reliable prompts state exactly what is wanted: the task, the audience, the length, and the format. Vague prompts force the model to guess, so specifying constraints removes ambiguity and makes the output far more consistent from run to run.

nestedTopics.title: Providing context
nestedTopics.explanation: Because the model only knows what is in the prompt plus its training, including the relevant background, data, or definitions it needs is essential. Missing context is a leading cause of wrong or generic answers, and supplying it is often more effective than any clever wording.

nestedTopics.title: Examples and format specification
nestedTopics.explanation: Showing one or more input-output examples, and explicitly stating the required output format, strongly biases the model toward producing exactly that shape. This is especially valuable when the output must be machine-readable, such as JSON that downstream code will parse.

followUps.question: What is the difference between zero-shot and few-shot prompting?
followUps.answer: Zero-shot prompting gives the model only the instruction and the task, with no worked examples, and relies on the model's general ability to figure out what to do. Few-shot prompting includes a handful of example input-output pairs in the prompt before the actual input, demonstrating the pattern you want. Few-shot often improves accuracy and format consistency for tricky or unusual tasks because the examples make the desired behavior concrete, but it costs more tokens. A common strategy is to start zero-shot for simplicity and add a few examples only when the model's output is unreliable or the format needs pinning down.

followUps.question: Why is specifying the output format so important for agents?
followUps.answer: Because in an agent, the model's output is usually consumed by code rather than read by a human, so it must be in a shape the code can parse reliably. If you leave the format loose, the model might wrap JSON in prose, vary field names, or add commentary, all of which break downstream parsing. Explicitly stating the format, and ideally providing an example or a schema, makes the output predictable and machine-readable. This is why structured output features and function schemas exist: they enforce the shape so the agent loop can dispatch on the result without fragile string parsing.

question: What is temperature and how does it affect model output?
directAnswer: Temperature is a sampling parameter that controls how random or deterministic the model's token choices are. A low temperature, near zero, makes the model pick the most probable tokens almost every time, producing focused, consistent, and repeatable output. A higher temperature flattens the probability distribution so less likely tokens have a better chance of being chosen, producing more varied and creative but less predictable output. You tune temperature to the task: low for factual, structured, or tool-driving work, higher for brainstorming or creative writing.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs:
Temperature scales the logits before the softmax that produces the probability distribution. Conceptually:
probs = softmax(logits / temperature)
A temperature below one sharpens the distribution toward the top tokens; above one flattens it so more tokens become plausible. At temperature zero the model effectively always takes the single most likely token.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Temperature exists to give you control over the trade-off between reliability and diversity. Some tasks need the safest, most probable continuation every time, such as extracting a value or emitting valid JSON, while others benefit from exploring less obvious options, such as generating varied ideas. One knob lets the same model serve both without changing the model itself.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Dividing the logits by the temperature before the softmax changes how peaked the resulting distribution is. A small temperature makes the largest logit dominate, so sampling almost always returns the top token, approaching greedy decoding. A large temperature shrinks the differences between logits, so probability spreads out and the sampler more often picks lower-ranked tokens, increasing variety and the chance of unusual or off-target output.

whyImportant: Temperature is one of the first knobs you reach for, and choosing it wrongly is a common cause of flaky agents or bland text. For tool-calling and structured output you generally want it low so behavior is stable and parseable. Interviewers ask this to confirm you understand that output randomness is a controllable design choice tied to the task's needs.
realWorldExample: An agent that must reliably decide which tool to call and format the arguments as JSON should run at a low temperature, so it consistently makes the correct, well-formed choice rather than occasionally improvising. By contrast, a feature that suggests three different marketing taglines benefits from a higher temperature so the suggestions are genuinely varied rather than three near-identical phrasings.

nestedTopics.title: Low temperature for reliability
nestedTopics.explanation: Setting temperature at or near zero makes the model strongly favor the highest-probability token, giving focused, consistent, and largely reproducible output. This is the right setting for extraction, classification, structured output, and tool calling, where you want the safest choice every time.

nestedTopics.title: High temperature for diversity
nestedTopics.explanation: Raising the temperature flattens the distribution so the model more readily picks less likely tokens, yielding more creative and varied output. It suits brainstorming and creative writing but increases the risk of drifting off task or producing errors, so it is used sparingly in agent control paths.

nestedTopics.title: Temperature versus top-p
nestedTopics.explanation: Temperature reshapes the whole distribution, while top-p (nucleus sampling) restricts choices to the smallest set of top tokens whose probabilities sum to a threshold. They are often used together, and both control randomness, but top-p caps which tokens are eligible rather than rescaling all of their probabilities.

followUps.question: Does temperature zero guarantee identical output every time?
followUps.answer: It makes output much more deterministic, but not always bit-for-bit identical in practice. At temperature zero the sampler picks the single highest-probability token at each step, so given the same prompt and model the logical output should be the same. However, real systems can still show small variations because of floating-point non-determinism on GPUs, differences in how requests are batched, model updates on the provider side, or ties broken inconsistently. For most purposes temperature zero gives you reproducible-enough behavior, and it's the right setting when you want consistency, but you should not assume it is a strict guarantee of identical bytes across every run.

followUps.question: How do temperature and top-p interact when both are set?
followUps.answer: They act as two stages of the same sampling process. Temperature first rescales the logits to make the distribution sharper or flatter, and then top-p (nucleus sampling) restricts the candidate set to the smallest group of top tokens whose cumulative probability reaches the threshold, discarding the long tail. The final token is sampled from that trimmed, rescaled distribution. Using both gives fine control, but it can also be confusing, so a common practice is to adjust one primarily, often temperature, and leave the other at a neutral default. For agent control paths you typically keep both conservative so behavior stays stable.
